read.sections.0.heading.back: Resources help people meet needs and wants
read.sections.0.heading.source: Resources help people meet needs and wants

read.sections.0.text.back: Every day, people make choices, from what they want to do after class to the way a family uses its food, money or phone data. To make these choices, people use resources. A resource is anything useful that people own, such as time, money, food, water, tools or skills. People use resources to meet their needs and wants. A need is something you must have to live safely and stay healthy, such as food, clean water and a safe place to sleep. A want is something you would like to own but you can still live without it. For example, Noor's aunt needs to buy rice and soap, but a new football is a want.

read.sections.1.text.back: Usually, people do not have enough resources for everything they need and want. This problem is called scarcity. Scarcity does not mean there is nothing; it means there is not enough for every possible use. Noor's family shares one phone with a little mobile data each week. Noor needs data for an online English class, and her cousins want to watch music videos. The data is not enough for both, so the family must make a decision. Communities also face scarcity. Hillside Learning Centre has one empty room on Tuesday afternoon, so the centre must choose between a homework club and an art class.

read.sections.2.heading.back: Every choice has an opportunity cost
read.sections.2.heading.source: Every choice has an opportunity cost

read.sections.2.text.note: Translator: 'Next-best option' is translated as 'pilihan kedua terbaik' (second-best choice), because a word-for-word 'terbaik seterusnya' sounds unnatural. Check this reads naturally. Back-translation check: 'Next-best option' is translated as 'pilihan kedua terbaik'. Check that this reads naturally and that the same wording works in the glossary, quick check feedback and watch summary.
read.sections.2.text.back: Every time you choose one thing, you give up something else. The second-best option that you give up is called the opportunity cost. On Saturday afternoon, Noor can play football with friends or practise English with a study partner. She chooses English, so her opportunity cost is the football game. Opportunity cost is not only about money; it can also be time, energy, space or other opportunities. Thinking about opportunity cost does not tell you which choice is right. Instead, it helps you understand what you are giving up. Before making a decision, ask: What do we need? What do we want? What will we give up?

read.sections.2.simpler.back: When you choose one thing, you give up another thing. The other best thing that you do not choose is the opportunity cost. On Saturday, Noor can play football. It does not tell the right choice. It shows what you give up.

watch.summary.back: This short video explains opportunity cost. When you choose one thing, you cannot get another thing. The second-best thing you give up is your opportunity cost. In this video, a young man named Mario needs a new phone. He also wants a new video game console. His money is not enough for both, so he has to choose. He could buy a cheaper phone and get both. But his phone would have fewer features. That is his opportunity cost. The video also shows that time can be a cost, not only money. The video says that the real cost of a choice is more than its price. Thinking about opportunity cost helps you compare needs and wants before making a decision.
watch.summary.source: This short video explains opportunity cost. When you pick one thing, you cannot have another. The next-best thing you give up is your opportunity cost. In the video, a young man called Mario needs a new phone. He also wants a new games console. His money is not enough for both, so he has to choose. He could buy a cheaper phone and get both things. But then his phone has fewer features. That is his opportunity cost. The video also shows that time can be a cost, not only money. It says the real cost of a choice is more than its price. Thinking about opportunity cost helps you compare needs and wants before you decide.
